sweep_summary: Goemai (goem1240) is not in the catalog. The single title-keyword hit, Gosson 2013 (Prosody and Iconicity, doi:10.1075/ill.13.11gos), is a French attitude-perception study; Glottolog's own record says its Goemai tag was assigned computationally from the word 'postural' in the title. Irrelevant, priority none. The first-hand stress statements for Goemai come from sources already downloaded in the prior pass: Tabain & Hellwig 2015 (JIPA, open access, full text held by the project) p. 87 states that a prosodically prominent ('stressed') open syllable is realized long and never as schwa 'independent of its position within a word', with no placement rule; Hellwig 2011 A Grammar of Goemai p. 51 (Google Books verbatim snippet only; book paywalled, readable at Harvard via the Harvard library catalogue) says stress patterns are 'inadequately understood and need further research' and that stress 'tends to fall on high-tone syllables'. Hellwig's 2003 thesis phonology section (scanned) is silent on stress. Recommended coding if added: tone language, word-stress position unpredictable/undescribed. Hellwig 2011 pp. 47-66 remains the one high-priority acquisition. New records and.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Goemai is a tone language (H, L, falling); the grammar recognises word stress but gives no positional rule: stress placement is declared inadequately understood, with the only generalisation that stress tends to coincide with high-toned syllables; a stressed open syllable may occur in any position in the word and is lengthened and never reduced, while short unstressed vowels of polysyllabic words reduce to schwa (schwa being most frequent in the initial CV syllable of CV.CV(V)(C) words, per the JIPA illustration).
new_statements.exceptions: None as such; author flags the whole topic as needing further research. Presentative and some other constructions raise the pitch register of H tones (intonational, not stress). Clause-final open syllables are also lengthened (p. 65), a separate boundary effect.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level: p. 61/JIPA explicitly frame the stressed syllable relative to 'its position within a word'; most Goemai words are monosyllabic, polysyllables arising from CV/N prefixes/proclitics, partial reduplication, pluractionals and compounds, so the question largely concerns CV.CV(V)(C) words. Statement read from verbatim Google Books snippets of pp. 51, 60-62, 66 (pages outside the viewable preview); the open-access JIPA text by the same author repeats the position-independence and schwa-reduction statements first-hand.
new_statements.identity_note: Hellwig's description is based mainly on the K'wo (Kwande) dialect of Goemai, with notes on Duut and Dorok dialect variation in vowels; all are Goemai proper (goem1240, ISO ank; older name Ankwe). The JIPA speaker (Louis Longpuan) is Hellwig's main K'wo consultant.

new_statements.reading: Goemai is a tone language (H, L, HL) with a phonetic stress/prominence category whose correlates are vowel length and non-reduction; the authors state explicitly that the stressed syllable is not fixed to a position in the word, and they give no placement rule. The reference grammar (Hellwig 2011: 51, read only as a verbatim Google Books snippet) says the stress patterns are 'inadequately understood and need further research' and that stress 'tends to fall on high-tone syllables'. For a word-stress catalog Goemai is therefore best coded as a tone language with no fixed/predictable word-stress position (stress placement unknown; tone-conditioned tendency), not as any positional stress type.

sources.note: Goemai is a tone language (H, L, HL contour; high-tone spreading, downdrift, phrase-final low). Stress ('prosodic prominence') exists as a phonetic category with correlates of vowel length and non-reduction, and it is explicitly not tied to a fixed position in the word. No placement rule is given; p. 92 adds that non-prominent syllables undergo vowel shortening/reduction, so polysyllables are mostly CV.CV(V)(C) with schwa in the initial syllable (which implies the initial syllable of such words is typically unstressed, but the authors do not say so directly).
